case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.answer: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions
case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       current conclusion may be unsafe."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

[Clinical case]
A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.
